title: Act V, Scene IV

teacherSummary.text: Young Cato, Portia's brother, proclaims his name and is killed. Lucilius pretends to be Brutus to protect him and is captured. Antony recognizes the trick, orders that Lucilius be treated kindly, and says he would rather have such men as friends than enemies.

This develops friendship and loyalty: Lucilius's loyalty. He cries "know me for Brutus," and Antony says he would "rather have / Such men my friends than enemies.".

The claim is persuasive only in part. In support, “I had rather have / Such men my friends than enemies” (Act V, Scene IV, Antony) bears it out: He cries "know me for Brutus," and Antony says he would "rather have / Such men my friends than enemies.". But “I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho” (Act V, Scene IV, Cato) complicates it, because this detail (young Cato) gives the reader a second explanation to weigh against the claim's reading. So the claim holds only once it is qualified: it explains much of the scene, but it has to account for that passage too, which it does not do on its own.

A model answer paraphrases the passage (Act V, Scene V, paragraph 38) accurately and quotes “Octavius” and “service”, saying what those words show about the speaker or situation at that moment.
